titre: The Paulette (1604): A Judge Who Owned His Office
accroche: In 1604, an annual tax lets French judicial officers pass their offices on to heirs. A fiscal expedient turns magistrates into owners.
contenu_vulgarise:
Under the Ancien Régime, a great many French magistrates were not appointed: they bought their office. The king sold judicial offices to fill his coffers, and the buyer became a judge by paying. Venality was not born in 1604, but that year it changed in nature.

The problem, from the buyer's point of view, was an old rule known as the forty-day rule. When an officer ceded his office to a successor, he had to survive forty days after resigning. If he died before then, the office reverted to the king, and the sum paid by the successor was lost. Buying an office from an old or sick man was therefore a gamble.

In 1604, under Henri IV, the monarchy offered a deal. Each year the officer paid the king a fee, the annual right (*droit annuel*). In exchange, he was exempted from the forty-day rule: his office could pass to an heir or a buyer with no risk of reverting to the king. The fee took the name Paulette, after Charles Paulet, secretary of the king's chamber, who devised it and was its first tax farmer, according to the *Encyclopédie*. The rate was initially on the order of one sixtieth of the office's value, according to historians; older texts give more complicated formulas, and the sources differ both on the exact calculation and on the day of the edict.

## A Fiscal Revenue That Creates a Class

For the king, the operation was a regular revenue stream: instead of collecting money only when an office was sold, he collected it every year. For officers, it was the security of property that could be bequeathed. Historians see it as one of the drivers behind the rise, at the head of the justice system, of the *noblesse de robe* (the nobility of the robe), a group of magistrates and families who handed offices down among themselves.

Nobody wanted this with any clarity: the Paulette was first of all a cash-flow expedient. It was a side effect, and it lasted nearly two centuries.

## When Justice Stops Being Property

On August 4, 1789, the night the National Assembly abolished privileges, article 7 of the decree suppressed the venality of judicial and municipal offices and laid down that justice would be rendered free of charge.

The Paulette thus shows an angle that histories of justice tend to forget: before asking whether a judge is impartial, one must ask who owns his post. When an office is property, the question of appointment becomes a question of inheritance.

In Stewart's English translation: “Venality of judicial and municipal offices is suppressed henceforth. Justice shall be rendered gratuitously.”

carte.punch: In 17th-century France, a judge could leave his office to his son.
carte.idee: In 1604, the Paulette, an annual fee paid to the king, exempts officers from the forty-day rule and makes their offices transmissible. A tax measure turns magistrates into owners of their posts, until August 4, 1789.
carte.source_courte: Edict of the Paulette, 1604 · Decrees of August 4, 1789

quiz.question: What does paying the annual fee, the Paulette, change for a judicial officer in 1604?
choix: He can pass on his office without risk of losing it if he dies within forty days of resigning
He receives a fixed salary from the king that replaces the sums paid by litigants
He becomes hereditarily noble as soon as he makes the first payment of the annual fee
He can sell his office back to the king at a price guaranteed by the edict when he retires
quiz.explication: The Paulette exempts the officer from the forty-day rule and makes the office transmissible. It sets no salary, does not confer nobility by itself, and guarantees no buyback by the king: it is a fiscal revenue for the monarchy.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who gave the Paulette its name, according to the entry?
choix: A magistrate of the Parlement of Paris
Charles Paulet, secretary of the king's chamber
The chancellor who drafted the edict of 1604
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The annual fee takes its name from Charles Paulet, secretary of the king's chamber, who devised it and was its first tax farmer, according to the *Encyclopédie*.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What was the Paulette's primary purpose for the monarchy?
choix: To found a hereditary nobility of the robe
To guarantee judges a fixed salary paid by the king
To fill the king's coffers with a regular annual revenue
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry presents the Paulette first of all as a cash-flow expedient: the king collects the fee every year, instead of collecting money only when an office is sold. The nobility of the robe is only a side effect.
